questions.stem: Which list gives Earth's layers from the centre outwards, with their states?
options: Solid silicate inner core, liquid metallic outer core, metallic mantle, silicate crust
Liquid silicate inner core, solid silicate outer core, metallic mantle, metallic crust
Solid metallic inner core, liquid metallic outer core, silicate mantle, silicate crust
Liquid metallic inner core, solid metallic outer core, silicate mantle, silicate crust
questions.explanation: Earth differentiated so that dense iron and nickel sank to form the core, with a solid inner core and liquid outer core. Lighter silicate rock makes up the mantle and crust. The inner core is solid despite its high temperature because of the enormous pressure.

questions.stem: Earth's average density is about 5.5 g/cm³, but rocks of the crust average about 2.7 to 3.0 g/cm³. What does this suggest?
options: Earth's interior must be hollow or filled mostly with gas under pressure
Earth's crust must be much thicker than the mantle and core together
Earth's interior must be made of the same rock as the surface crust
Earth's interior must contain material much denser than the crust
questions.explanation: If the whole planet averages 5.5 g/cm³ and the outer rocks are much lighter, the interior must be far denser. This fits a metallic iron-nickel core beneath a silicate mantle and crust.

questions.stem: How do P-waves and S-waves differ?
options: P-waves travel only through liquids; S-waves travel only through gases
Both travel through solids only, but S-waves arrive at stations first
P-waves travel through solids and liquids; S-waves travel only through solids
S-waves travel through solids and liquids; P-waves travel only through solids
questions.explanation: P-waves are compressional waves that pass through solids, liquids and gases and travel fastest, so they arrive first. S-waves are shear waves that cannot travel through liquids, because liquids cannot resist shearing.

questions.stem: Seismometers more than about 103° of arc from an earthquake's focus record no direct S-waves. What does this S-wave shadow zone show?
options: The outer core is liquid, so it stops S-waves from passing through
The inner core is liquid, so it absorbs both P-waves and S-waves
The mantle is liquid, so it stops S-waves close to the surface
The crust is too thin there, so S-waves leave Earth into space
questions.explanation: S-waves cannot pass through liquids, so a large area on the far side of Earth receives no direct S-waves. This shows that a liquid layer, the outer core, lies deep inside. The mantle transmits S-waves, so it is solid.

questions.stem: P-waves are recorded both near an earthquake and on the far side of Earth, but not in a band between about 103° and 142° from the focus. What causes this P-wave shadow zone?
options: P-waves are reflected at the crust, so they travel back towards the earthquake
P-waves slow down in the inner core until they stop before reaching the surface
P-waves are refracted where they enter the core, bending them away from that band
P-waves are stopped by the liquid outer core, so none reach the far side of Earth
questions.explanation: P-waves do pass through the liquid core, which is why they reach the far side. Their sudden slowing at the core-mantle boundary refracts them sharply, leaving a ring where no direct P-waves arrive. Stopping waves completely is the behaviour of S-waves, not P-waves.

questions.stem: Seismic wave speeds increase suddenly at a depth of a few tens of kilometres beneath the continents. What does this discontinuity mark?
options: The boundary between the crust and the mantle
The boundary between the mantle and the outer core
The boundary between the outer and inner core
The boundary between the oceans and the crust
questions.explanation: The Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho, is where seismic waves speed up as they pass from crustal rock into denser mantle rock. It lies at roughly 30 to 70 km under continents and is much shallower under oceans. The core-mantle boundary is about 2900 km down.

questions.stem: At a depth of about 2900 km, P-wave speed drops sharply and S-waves disappear. Which interpretation is best supported?
options: Solid mantle rock gives way to a liquid metallic outer core
Liquid mantle rock gives way to a solid metallic outer core
Solid mantle rock gives way to a hollow region filled with gas
Solid crustal rock gives way to a partly molten upper mantle
questions.explanation: S-waves stop because the layer below is liquid, and P-waves slow because liquid transmits compression more slowly. Together these mark the core-mantle boundary. A gas-filled cavity is ruled out because P-waves still pass through and the density data require dense material.

questions.stem: Iron meteorites are made mostly of iron and nickel, and stony meteorites are made of silicate minerals. How do they provide evidence for Earth's interior?
options: They prove the core is solid throughout, because iron meteorites are solid when they land
They are thought to come from early bodies that separated into metal cores and rocky mantles
They fell into Earth's core and were later thrown back to the surface by volcanic eruptions
They show that Earth's core is made of silicate minerals like those in stony meteorites
questions.explanation: Meteorites are leftovers from the formation of the solar system. Iron meteorites are thought to come from the cores of broken bodies that separated into metal and rock, supporting the idea that Earth's core is iron-nickel. Their solid state on landing says nothing about the state of Earth's core.

questions.stem: Why does the model of Earth's interior rely on evidence from many international organisations?
options: A worldwide network of seismic stations is needed to record waves at many distances
Each country owns a different layer of the interior and studies only that layer
International organisations drill deep holes that sample the mantle and core
One seismometer can record everything, but the data must be stored overseas
questions.explanation: Shadow zones and changes in wave speed are only detected by comparing records from stations spread around the world, so international data sharing is essential. No borehole has reached the mantle, let alone the core.

questions.stem: Felsic minerals are rich in which elements?
options: Magnesium and iron with little silicon
Calcium and carbon with no silicon
Iron and nickel with no oxygen at all
Silicon, aluminium, sodium and potassium
questions.explanation: Felsic minerals, such as quartz and potassium feldspar, are rich in silica together with aluminium, sodium and potassium, and are usually light coloured. Minerals rich in magnesium and iron are mafic.

questions.stem: Which group of minerals is mafic?
options: Calcite and halite
Olivine and pyroxene
Quartz and muscovite
Orthoclase and quartz
questions.explanation: Olivine and pyroxene are rich in magnesium and iron and are dark and dense, so they are mafic. Quartz, muscovite and orthoclase feldspar are felsic. Calcite and halite are not silicate minerals.

questions.stem: A coarse-grained igneous rock is pale pink and grey, with abundant quartz and feldspar crystals visible to the naked eye. What is it?
options: Granite, a felsic plutonic rock
Basalt, a mafic volcanic rock
Gabbro, a mafic plutonic rock
Rhyolite, a felsic volcanic rock
questions.explanation: Large crystals mean slow cooling underground (plutonic), and abundant quartz and feldspar mean a felsic composition, so the rock is granite. Rhyolite has the same composition but is fine-grained because it cooled quickly at the surface.

questions.stem: Why do volcanic igneous rocks such as basalt have much smaller crystals than plutonic rocks such as gabbro of the same composition?
options: Plutonic rocks cool quickly underground, so their crystals grow larger
Volcanic rocks are reheated later, which breaks their crystals apart
Lava cools quickly at the surface, leaving little time for crystals to grow
Lava contains fewer elements, so fewer types of crystals can form
questions.explanation: Crystal size depends mainly on cooling rate. Magma deep underground cools slowly, allowing large crystals to grow, while lava erupted at the surface cools quickly and forms small crystals or glass. Basalt and gabbro have the same mafic composition.

questions.stem: A volcanic rock is black, glassy and breaks with smooth curved surfaces, with no visible crystals. How did it form?
options: Lava cooled slowly in a thick flow, so crystals grew very large
Lava cooled so quickly that crystals had no time to form
Magma cooled very slowly deep underground over thousands of years
Sediment was buried and heated until all of its grains melted
questions.explanation: This describes obsidian, volcanic glass formed when lava cools almost instantly, so atoms cannot arrange into crystals. Slow cooling produces large crystals, the opposite texture.

questions.stem: Which list contains only clastic sedimentary rocks?
options: Conglomerate, sandstone and shale
Coal, coquina and chalk
Rock salt, gypsum and chert
Marble, slate and quartzite
questions.explanation: Clastic rocks are made of fragments of older rock, sorted by grain size: conglomerate (gravel), sandstone (sand) and shale (clay and silt). Coal, coquina and chalk are organic, rock salt and gypsum are chemical, and marble, slate and quartzite are metamorphic.

questions.stem: Rock salt forms when seawater in a shallow lagoon evaporates. How is rock salt classified?
options: An organic sedimentary rock
A clastic sedimentary rock
A contact metamorphic rock
A chemical sedimentary rock
questions.explanation: Rock salt forms when dissolved ions crystallise out of water as it evaporates, so it is a chemical sedimentary rock. It contains no broken rock fragments (clastic) and is not made from the remains of organisms (organic).

questions.stem: Coal forms from thick layers of plant material that accumulated in swamps and were buried. How is coal classified?
options: An organic sedimentary rock
A chemical sedimentary rock
A clastic sedimentary rock
A regional metamorphic rock
questions.explanation: Coal is made from the compressed remains of plants, so it is an organic (biogenic) sedimentary rock. Chemical sedimentary rocks crystallise directly from solution, and clastic rocks are made of rock fragments.

questions.stem: A sedimentary rock contains large, angular fragments of several rock types in a fine matrix, poorly sorted. Which is the most likely origin?
options: Rapid deposition close to the source, such as at the foot of a cliff
Long transport by a river, which rounded and sorted the grains
Slow settling of fine mud in the still water of a deep lake
Wind transport across a desert, which sorted the grains by size
questions.explanation: Angular, poorly sorted fragments (a breccia) have not travelled far, because transport rounds and sorts grains. Deposition near the source, such as rockfall at the base of a cliff, fits best. Wind and long river transport produce well-sorted, rounded grains.

questions.stem: A sample fizzes strongly when a drop of dilute hydrochloric acid is placed on it. Which mineral does this indicate?
options: Olivine
Calcite
Quartz
Feldspar
questions.explanation: Calcite (calcium carbonate) reacts with dilute acid to release carbon dioxide bubbles, so the test identifies carbonate rocks such as limestone and marble. Quartz, feldspar and olivine are silicates and do not fizz.

questions.stem: Contact metamorphism occurs when:
options: Rock is broken into fragments that are carried away and deposited elsewhere
Rock is heated by a nearby body of magma, without intense directed pressure
Rock is squeezed over a huge area as mountains form at a plate boundary
Rock is ground and sheared along a fault as blocks move past each other
questions.explanation: Contact metamorphism is caused mainly by heat from an intrusion, affecting a zone around it, and produces non-foliated rocks such as hornfels. Large-scale squeezing during mountain building is regional metamorphism, and shearing along faults is dynamic metamorphism.

questions.stem: Shale is buried deep beneath a growing mountain range and subjected to rising temperature and pressure. Which sequence of rocks forms as metamorphism increases?
options: Schist, then slate, then hornfels
Slate, then schist, then gneiss
Gneiss, then schist, then slate
Marble, then quartzite, then slate
questions.explanation: In regional metamorphism, shale becomes slate at low grade, then schist and finally gneiss at high grade, with minerals growing larger and foliation becoming more pronounced. Marble and quartzite form from limestone and sandstone.

questions.stem: Which metamorphic rock forms from limestone?
options: Marble
Quartzite
Slate
Gneiss
questions.explanation: Heating limestone recrystallises its calcite into an interlocking mosaic, forming marble, which still fizzes in acid. Quartzite forms from quartz sandstone, and slate and gneiss form from shale or other fine rocks.

questions.stem: A rock collected from a major fault zone has a streaky, finely ground texture with stretched mineral grains, but nearby rocks away from the fault are unchanged. What type of metamorphism produced it?
options: Dynamic metamorphism caused by shearing along the fault
Contact metamorphism caused by heat from a nearby intrusion
Regional metamorphism caused by burial across a wide area
Chemical weathering caused by water moving along the fault
questions.explanation: Intense shearing where rock masses move past each other grinds and stretches grains, producing rocks such as mylonite in a narrow zone along the fault. Regional metamorphism affects wide areas, and contact metamorphism is centred on an intrusion.

questions.stem: A student uses a flow chart and hand lens to classify a fine-grained dark rock as basalt, but a teacher says it could be a dark hornfels. Which limitation of the tools does this show?
options: Flow charts never work for igneous rocks, because their minerals are always too large to see
Hand lenses change the colour of minerals, so colour cannot be used to classify any rock
Basalt and hornfels have identical origins, so the classification makes no difference
Very fine grains cannot be seen with a hand lens, so a thin section or other test may be needed
questions.explanation: When grains are too small to identify by eye or hand lens, rocks with different origins can look alike. Thin sections under a microscope or chemical analysis resolve this. Basalt is volcanic and hornfels is metamorphic, so the difference matters.

questions.stem: Which is an example of physical (mechanical) weathering?
options: Iron minerals in a rock reacting with oxygen to form rust
Feldspar crystals reacting with water to form clay minerals
Water freezing in a crack and wedging the rock apart
Carbonic acid in rain dissolving a limestone outcrop
questions.explanation: Frost wedging breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its minerals, so it is physical weathering. Dissolving limestone, oxidising iron and turning feldspar into clay all change the minerals chemically.

questions.stem: Feldspar in granite slowly reacts with water to form clay minerals, leaving quartz grains behind. What does this show?
options: Erosion turns quartz into clay once it has been carried by a river
Chemical weathering only affects rocks that contain calcium carbonate
Chemical weathering alters some minerals but leaves resistant quartz
Physical weathering breaks all minerals into clay at the same rate
questions.explanation: Feldspar is broken down chemically (hydrolysis) into clays, while quartz resists chemical weathering and remains as sand grains. This is why granite weathers to a sandy, clay-rich soil.

questions.stem: Weathering and erosion are often confused. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
options: Weathering moves rock fragments away; erosion breaks the rock down in place
Weathering only happens in deserts; erosion only happens in wet climates
Weathering is caused only by living things; erosion only by moving ice
Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion moves the weathered material away
questions.explanation: Weathering is the breakdown of rock at or near the surface without significant movement. Erosion is the removal and transport of that material by water, wind, ice or gravity. Both happen in all climates.

questions.stem: Why does soil formation require interaction between the geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere?
options: Only rock and water are needed, because the atmosphere and organisms play no part in soils
Organisms make soil directly from air, so rock and water contribute little to the process
Rock supplies minerals, air and water drive weathering, and organisms add organic matter and mix the soil
Rock supplies organic matter, air supplies minerals, and water stops organisms from living in soil
questions.explanation: Soil forms as parent rock (geosphere) is weathered by water and atmospheric gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide, while plants, microbes and burrowing animals (biosphere) add organic matter and break up and mix the material. All four spheres contribute.

questions.stem: Which list best describes the components of a typical healthy soil?
options: Organic matter and air only, with very little mineral material
Rock fragments and living organisms only, with no water or air
Mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms
Mineral particles and water only, with no air or organic matter
questions.explanation: Soil is a mixture of weathered rock and mineral particles, organic matter, water and air in the pore spaces, and organisms such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms. In a typical good soil, mineral particles make up the largest share by volume.

questions.stem: A soil sample is 20% sand, 20% silt and 60% clay. Using a soil texture triangle, how is it classified?
options: Clay
Loam
Sand
Silt loam
questions.explanation: With 60% clay, the soil falls in the clay region at the top of the triangle, which covers soils with 40% or more clay and less than 40% silt and 45% sand. A loam has a much more even mix, with less than about 27% clay.

questions.stem: Using a soil texture triangle, a sample has 35% sand and 25% clay. What percentage of silt does it contain?
questions.explanation: The three fractions of a soil texture triangle always add to 100%, so silt = 100 − 35 − 25 = 40%. A mix of 35% sand, 40% silt and 25% clay falls in the loam class.

questions.stem: Soil X is 90% sand. Soil Y is 40% sand, 40% silt and 20% clay. Which comparison is most likely to be correct?
options: X and Y hold the same amount of water, because both contain sand
Y drains faster than X, because silt grains are larger than sand
X drains faster but holds less water and fewer nutrients than Y
X holds more water and more nutrients than Y, but drains slower
questions.explanation: Sandy soils have large pores, so water drains quickly and few nutrients are held. Loams such as Y have a mix of particle sizes, with clay that holds water and nutrient ions. Silt grains are smaller than sand grains, not larger.

questions.stem: A student dries a 50.0 g soil sample in an oven until its mass is constant at 40.0 g. What is the moisture content as a percentage of the dry mass?
questions.explanation: The water lost is 50.0 − 40.0 = 10.0 g. As a percentage of the dry mass, this is 10.0 ÷ 40.0 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by the wet mass instead gives 20%, which is a different measure.

questions.stem: To measure organic content, a dried soil sample is heated strongly in a crucible and weighed again. Why does its mass decrease?
options: Clay minerals melt and run out of the bottom of the crucible
Sand grains evaporate at the high temperature of the flame
Air in the pore spaces is driven out as a gas
Organic matter burns off as carbon dioxide and water vapour
questions.explanation: Strong heating burns the organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and water vapour, so the loss in mass estimates organic content. Sand and clay minerals remain at these temperatures, and the air in pores has negligible mass.

questions.stem: In much of the Brigalow Belt of central Queensland, brigalow forest grows on heavy clay soils that crack deeply when dry. Why can soil maps of Australia be based partly on native vegetation?
options: Native plants grow only on bare rock, so they show where soils are absent
Native plant communities are closely correlated with particular soil types
Native plants create soils from the air, so they decide which soil forms
Native vegetation is the same on every soil type, so it is easy to map
questions.explanation: Particular native plant communities are adapted to particular soils, so vegetation is a useful indicator of soil type, as with brigalow on cracking clays. Many soil maps were built using this correlation together with field sampling.

questions.stem: A soil sample forms a long, sticky ribbon when moistened and pressed between the fingers, has a pH of 8.5 and very little organic matter. It swells when wet and cracks when dry. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
options: A reactive clay soil that could damage house foundations and may need management for farming
A sandy soil with a high organic content that is ideal for building foundations
A loam soil with a neutral pH that needs no management for farming or building
A silty soil with acid pH that will not change in volume when its water content changes
questions.explanation: A long ribbon indicates high clay content, and swelling and cracking indicate a reactive (shrink-swell) clay, which can crack foundations and roads. The alkaline pH and low organic matter also limit soil quality for some crops. Sandy soils form short ribbons or none.

questions.stem: Which combination of properties indicates the best soil quality for growing most crops?
options: Platy, compacted structure, high salt content and a pH of about 10
Good crumb structure, moderate organic content and a pH of about 6 to 7
Massive structure, no organic content and a pH of about 4
Loose single grains, no organic content and a pH of about 9.5
questions.explanation: A crumbly (granular) structure lets air and water move, organic matter holds water and nutrients and feeds soil life, and a near-neutral pH keeps most nutrients available. Very acid or alkaline, compacted or salty soils limit plant growth.
